Get altitude data

Markus Bauer

Source: vignettes/altitude-vignette.Rmd
altitude-vignette.Rmd

This vignette shows how to add altitude to the header table for resy_classify(). The elevation map is too large to be included in the package, so you need to download it separately.

Whether you need altitude depends on the expert system. In the EUNIS expert system (version 2025-10-03), for example, 15 habitat types use altitude: snow-bed vegetation (R41) and Iberian summer pasture (R24), alpine and subalpine scrub (S21, S22, S23, S25, S26), dry heath (S42), mountain forests (T1C, T1D, T31, T32, T34, T37) and coniferous plantations of non site-native trees (T3M).

If your data already records altitude, in a column Altitude (m) or Altitude, or as the Darwin Core columns minimumElevationInMeters and maximumElevationInMeters, RESY uses it directly and you do not need this vignette.

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(here)
library(sf)
library(terra)
library(tidyterra)

Example

The example uses a small part of the elevation map and the example plots that lie in it.

Load data

Load the altitude data for the example area:

altitude <- terra::rast(
  system.file("extdata", "data_example_altitude.tif", package = "RESY")
)
altitude
#> class       : SpatRaster
#> size        : 63, 168, 1  (nrow, ncol, nlyr)
#> resolution  : 0.0005555556, 0.0005555556  (x, y)
#> extent      : 10.69171, 10.78504, 44.12662, 44.16162  (xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax)
#> coord. ref. : lon/lat WGS 84 (EPSG:4326)
#> source      : data_example_altitude.tif
#> name        : eurodem
#> min value   :     771
#> max value   :    1927

Load the example plots that lie in this area:

data_sites <- readr::read_csv(
  system.file("extdata", "data_example_sites.csv", package = "RESY"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
) |>
  dplyr::select(PlotObservationID, Longitude, Latitude) |>
  sf::st_as_sf(coords = c("Longitude", "Latitude"), crs = 4326) |>
  sf::st_transform(terra::crs(altitude)) |>
  sf::st_crop(sf::st_bbox(altitude)) # the example uses part of the map

The map shows the altitude and the example plots (red):

ggplot() +
  tidyterra::geom_spatraster(data = altitude) +
  tidyterra::scale_fill_whitebox_c(
    palette = "high_relief",
    na.value = "lightblue"
    ) +
  geom_sf(data = data_sites, color = "red", size = 2) +
  labs(fill = "Altitude (m)") +
  theme_classic()

© EuroGeographics 2026, Istituto Geografico Militare (IGM), Italy; Licence

Get Altitude (m)

terra::extract() returns the value of the raster at each plot, in a column named after the raster layer, here eurodem. Any elevation raster in meters works the same way, for example a national elevation model; use its layer name in place of eurodem.

data_sites <- data_sites |>
  mutate(
    "Altitude (m)" = terra::extract(altitude, terra::vect(data_sites))$eurodem
    )
data_sites
#> Simple feature collection with 8 features and 2 fields
#> Geometry type: POINT
#> Dimension:     XY
#> Bounding box:  xmin: 10.70124 ymin: 44.12676 xmax: 10.78004 ymax: 44.15539
#> Geodetic CRS:  WGS 84
#> # A tibble: 8 × 3
#>   PlotObservationID            geometry `Altitude (m)`
#> * <chr>                     <POINT [°]>          <dbl>
#> 1 VG30              (10.73782 44.15088)           1434
#> 2 JW66              (10.73688 44.15539)           1657
#> 3 MJ41              (10.73647 44.14837)           1355
#> 4 WH80              (10.70124 44.15468)           1765
#> 5 DS96              (10.78004 44.12676)           1645
#> 6 SB81              (10.77721 44.13099)           1640
#> 7 JU84               (10.7681 44.13086)           1507
#> 8 KM11              (10.77537 44.13324)           1690

A plot outside the raster, or over the sea, gets NA. resy_classify() evaluates a missing altitude as 0 m and warns with the number of such plots, so a mountain plot without altitude can fail a rule such as “higher than 1000 m”. The same happens to all plots when the header table has no altitude column. Check for missing values before classifying:

sum(is.na(data_sites$`Altitude (m)`))
#> [1] 0

Add Altitude (m) to the header table

resy_classify() reads the altitude from the header table, which has one row per plot. Dropping the geometry from data_sites gives such a table. If you already have a header table, join the new column to it by PlotObservationID.

header <- sf::st_drop_geometry(data_sites)
head(header)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 2
#>   PlotObservationID `Altitude (m)`
#>   <chr>                      <dbl>
#> 1 VG30                        1434
#> 2 JW66                        1657
#> 3 MJ41                        1355
#> 4 WH80                        1765
#> 5 DS96                        1645
#> 6 SB81                        1640

Crop your own altitude data

Download EuroDEM (European Digital Elevation Model), an elevation map of Europe by EuroGeographics, co-funded by the European Union, from https://www.mapsforeurope.org/datasets/euro-dem.

The code in this section needs the downloaded file, so it is not run when this vignette is built.

Load altitude data

Save EuroDEM data in the data folder of your R project. From there, you can load the raster file.

altitude <- terra::rast(
  here::here("data", "euro-dem-tif", "data", "eurodem.tif")
)

EuroDEM stores its extent in arcseconds; dividing by 3600 converts it to degrees.

e <- terra::ext(altitude)
terra::ext(altitude) <- terra::ext(
  e[1] / 3600, e[2] / 3600, e[3] / 3600, e[4] / 3600
)

The altitude data needs the right coordinate reference system: EPSG:4258, ETRS89 (European Terrestrial Reference System 1989) in degrees.

terra::crs(altitude) <- "EPSG:4258"  # geographic ETRS89, degrees

Get an overview of the status of the EuroDEM data.

altitude

Load your sites

Load your sites data, with the columns PlotObservationID, Longitude and Latitude, transform it to an sf object and align its coordinate reference system with the altitude raster.

data_sites <- readr::read_csv(
  here::here("data", "data_sites.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
) |>
  sf::st_as_sf(coords = c("Longitude", "Latitude"), crs = 4326) |>
  sf::st_transform(terra::crs(altitude))

Crop to your area

Crop the elevation map to the area covered by your vegetation relevés:

altitude_cropped <- data_sites |>
  sf::st_buffer(0.5) |> # degrees now, ~50 km
  sf::st_bbox() |>
  terra::crop(x = altitude, y = _) |>
  terra::project("EPSG:4326")

Save the cropped and therefore smaller altitude data for later use.

terra::writeRaster(
  altitude_cropped,
  here::here("data", "data_altitude.tif"),
  overwrite = TRUE
)

Now you can go on with the above example and get altitude data, loading data_altitude.tif in place of the example file.
